Industry News: Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between.
  • According to recent reports, I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher.
  • It has been revealed that I was a bagger at Kroger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith as the Upcoming York-based fashion house celebrates its 30th anniversary. Smith has spent more than two decades at the helm of the brand, working her way up from a part-time freelancer to creative lead. But her fashion ambitions began long before she arrived in New York. Growing up in Atlanta, she ran her own neighborhood art camp before discovering designers like Donna Karan and realizing fashion could be a career. Now, Smith is celebrating the women who have shaped Lafayette 148 through its “Uniform” campaign, which highlights accomplished New Yorkers and their individual approaches to personal style. Below, Smith reflects on her unconventional start, why she’s stayed at the company for over 20 years, and the career advice she wishes she’d followed sooner.

According to recent reports, I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher. It was basically babysitting all the neighborhood kids, but I created a flyer, got paid for it, and did the whole thing. I started in second grade, and we did it every year for about eight years. I even started hiring people so we could have two classes going at once. We had swimming lessons. The local news even came and did a segment on it. I loved decorating my classroom and setting everything up. My parents were so nice to give me the garage and basement to do it all. Not necessarily an official job, but my first money-making moment.

It has been revealed that I was a bagger at Kroger. It just was not for me.

I was always creative growing up. At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan. It’s kind of crazy when you see somebody doing something and suddenly realize, Oh, that’s a career. I can do that. I became obsessed with everything in the ’90s, all the Upcoming York fashion at the time. That was when I decided I wanted to pursue it. When college applications came around, my mom really encouraged me to go to art school. I started in fashion, and that became my focus. Growing up in Atlanta, I wasn’t necessarily surrounded by a significant fashion community. But my dad’s office was across the street from the art museum at one point, and I remember going there and having that exposure. My mom was always crafty and creative, too. She really encouraged us to be who we were.

There’s a language creative people have that’s a little different from the way business people communicate. When I went to art school, I felt like I’d found my people. It wasn’t just fashion people. It was photographers, fine artists, and all these different kinds of creatives. Being around people who thought about things differently was really inspiring. Even today, I thrive around people who have creative insight. There’s always a little more depth to the way they see things.

Industry observers note that I interned at Bill Blass for about six months. I moved to New York in July 2001, and we had our fashion show on September 10. I remember Marc Jacobs had his show that day, too, and everybody was celebrating. People were saying, “Just come a little late to work tomorrow.” And then, obviously, September 11 happened. A week later, the entire team was let go, from the top down. What I learned from that experience was the fragility of everything. Don’t take anything for granted. Anything can come and go in a moment. But I also worked with Lars Nilsson and Hervé Pierre Braillard, who were just the kindest people. This industry has a little bit of everything, but I loved that they led with kindness, even when they were under so much pressure. As an intern, I was literally carrying ironing boards down the street and doing a sketch here or there. It was very much about doing whatever needed to be done.

After my internship, I had a brief stint of freelancing. Those were some long months. I remember coming home from one job and my roommates asking how my day was. I said, “Well, I was putting pigs on socks.” I knew I wouldn’t be going back. Freelancing is hard. It’s a grind, but you meet a lot of great people. I actually made some really good contacts during that time. I eventually met Deirdre [Quinn], Lafayette 148’s founder. She met with me on a Saturday, which I thought was incredible. I was really just looking for advice. I wasn’t looking for a job, and I didn’t even know much about the brand. It was only five years old. She was so kind, full of knowledge, and passionate. After I spent a year freelancing and meeting people who seemed so over the industry, her enthusiasm reminded me why I wanted to do this in the first place. She offered me a part-time freelance position, and the rest is history.

In a recent development, in the beginning, security was really important to me. The idea of losing a job and having to pay rent was scary, so that was definitely part of it initially. But really, it was the growth. Within a couple of years, they were sending me to the factory. It was a small, tight-knit firm, so I was able to wear a lot of different hats. I had a mentor named Barbara Gast who was traveling back and forth from Italy, and I was learning so much from her. I’d compare notes with friends in the industry and realize how much hands-on experience I was getting. I understood the value of that and really loved being so close to the product. It never got boring. And whenever things did get slightly boring, I’d ask, “Okay, what’s next?” And there was always something. It’s such an entrepreneurial place that you can almost create your next opportunity. That’s what made it so exciting.

I think if you asked Deirdre, she’d have a different answer because she has her own experience of building the company. For me, it’s about having started at a company that was really a factory and being part of the journey of building its identity and what it stands for. I was the kid running up and down the factory floors collecting samples. That hustle and bustle was so innate to who the brand was. To me, it was really exciting to build more of a brand story around that. Thirty years later, we’re still celebrating those roots and making sure we haven’t strayed too far from them, while continuing to evolve. Being part of that journey has been really exciting.

The constant has always been this idea of an accomplished woman. She’s always been at the forefront of who we’re designing for. At the time, it was the career woman. But now, what does that even mean anymore? What does that look like? There are so many different versions of that woman and so many different ways people dress. At the heart of it, she’s a woman who knows what she wants. She’s busy and has a really full life, whether she’s starting her career or ending it. They can all find something in the clothes.

Recent findings suggest that for us, it was about choosing people who inspire us. Number one, they had to be New York women. That was the base. We wanted women who make us want to be better ourselves. From someone like Deborah Berke, the architect, to women who have built incredible careers in other fields, it’s vital to shine a light on them. I think back to when I was a kid and how much you need that kind of inspiration. Even at a certain stage in your career, when you’re wondering what the point is, it’s nice to have people who inspire you. These are women who have really built something for themselves, and I think that’s worth celebrating.

Sources indicate that sophie de Rakoff noted something during the project that I really liked, and I’m going to steal it: “Dressing with intention.” When you know yourself, you know what works on you. It’s no longer about dressing to impress. There’s a confidence in knowing what works for you and making it work. We’re all so busy. Who has time to overthink getting dressed? You know what works, and you build a system around that. You’re able to create a wardrobe that really works for you. Everybody has a different definition of a uniform, and that was the whole point of the project.

In a recent development, when I first started in the industry, I was a total hippie. I was making my own clothes, and they were terrible. Absolutely falling apart. It was what it was. I think part of the change comes from not having as much time as you did when you were younger. But it’s also about simplicity and comfort. I know that if I’m going to be on the floor pinning something but also have to give a presentation, there are certain pieces that work for both. I can be comfortable and still feel appropriately dressed. I’ve found a handful of things that work for me, and I don’t have to think too much about them anymore. A crisp, oversize white cotton button-down is half my closet. I also love a soft skirt and a significant chunky sweater. Those are the pieces I always go back to and interchange depending on the day. I even wear sweaters in the summer. It’s cold in the Navy Yard!

Our pants fit incredibly well. The moment somebody gets into our pants, they’ll love us forever. Then it’s the jacket and the white shirt. Those three things are our gateway pieces, and everything else follows. You need a good blazer and a good leather piece, too. Once you find those foundational pieces that really work for you, everything else becomes easier.

I really want to see more women in our clothes. It’s not just about growing the business. It makes me happy when I see people put on our clothes and feel really good. We work so hard to make sure things fit the way a woman wants them to fit. I just want more people to enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Sources indicate that yesterday, Hailey Bieber took her obsession with ’90s minimalism one step further with a reference to the ultimate ‘90s minimalist: Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy. For a talk at the 2026 DealBook Summit here in New York, she and her stylist Dani Michelle pulled a Yohji Yamamoto look from Spring 1998, the one with a black, high-necked jacket with a line of delicate buttons paired with a white linen column skirt so famously worn by CBK in June 1998. It did what it was supposed to do: Stop us in our scrolling. But it jogged something else in the collective consciousness of fashion lovers everywhere. Hadn’t this jacket just made the rounds on our feeds?

According to recent reports, A few weeks ago, savvy shoppers spotted the look for sale on the RealReal. Bessette-Kennedy’s reverence for Yohji Yamamoto is one that fashion’s acolytes tend to share, so it didn’t take long for the listing to go viral. The description identified its starry provenance: “From the Spring/Summer 1998 Collection; as worn by Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in 1998 and worn by Winona Ryder for the season 5 premiere of 'Stranger Things' in 2025.”.

Industry observers note that TRR listed the jacket for $7,025. It sat on the site long enough to make the Instagram rounds, but someone snatched it up before the site had time to mark it down. The jacket sold for full price on November 6, less than two weeks before the DealBook Summit.

Recent findings suggest that could it be that Bieber scrolls for vintage Yohji on the RealReal like the rest of us? Does she have saved searches? Is she watching her obsessions with the eyes of a hawk? (Or has she outsourced this job to Michelle or someone on her team?) Bazaar reached out to the RealReal, and a spokesperson revealed that while all customer data is private, they know that Bieber’s look did not come from them. Well, it was fun to imagine. But just the possibility that this could have happened is enough to make you think.

Michelle’s post of the look does not reveal her source, though days later, she confirmed the source to be Tab Vintage. The vintage resale platform Shy mentioned in comment sections that it recently sold the same piece. Another one of the jackets, also without a proven link to CBK’s personal wardrobe, sold via the Fashion Auctioneer in March for $12,500. That’s the thing with ready-to-wear: It’s not one-of-a-kind. Bessette-Kennedy bought her jacket off the rack, which means there are multiple versions floating around out there.

If you scroll down the jacket’s sold page on the RealReal to the “Related Items” section, you’ll find multiple listings of the Cruise 2005 Chanel jacket Andy Sachs famously wore in The Devil Wears Prada, priced at roughly ten grand. “Similar style seen on Anne Hathaway in 'The Devil Wears Prada,'” the description reads. “We are seeing more and more archival pieces with incredible cultural provenance come in on consignment,” says Kristen Naiman, chief brand officer at the RealReal. “And we love helping these shards of fashion history resurface in pop culture.”.

It’s become common practice for major stylists to mine specialty vintage stores for these megawatt, nostalgia-driven red carpet references. Just look at Law Roach’s Instagram account, where he documents pulling 1950s Balenciaga for Kim Kardashian from Lily et Cie, a source that specializes in museum-quality vintage. But as this thought experiment exemplifies, these transactions are becoming more normalized.

Sources indicate that naiman continues: “Whether you know Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy or not, there is now an entire upcoming generation coveting this Yohji Yamamoto look on Hailey Bieber, and it has a renewed desirability because of that. And that’s the fun of being a fashion hobbyist and TRR enthusiast. You not only love the piece, you know the love story behind the piece. It’s a way to participate in fashion history. You can spend years coveting a jacket that has left an indelible mark on culture and then, one day, find it in your size.”.

Which brings us back to that Yohji jacket that sold on November 6. We know Bieber wasn’t the one who purchased it, but some lucky person did, and now they own a piece of fashion history. Wonder how many other people have the same one.

Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore are country music’s newest couple.

Sources indicate that after months of speculation about their relationship, multiple sources confirmed to People on Sept. 23, 2026, that Langley and Wetmore are dating. The news came one day after the two country singers attended the Nashville Songwriter Awards, where Langley celebrated another major moment in her career.

Sources indicate that neither Langley nor Wetmore has publicly commented on their relationship yet. But their history goes back to at least late 2025, when they began appearing at some of the same industry events before sparking dating rumors during a trip to the British Virgin Islands that December. Since then, they’ve also shared the stage.

Below, a full timeline of everything we know about Langley and Wetmore’s relationship so far.

Sources indicate that langley and Wetmore were both at the BMI Country Awards in Nashville on November 18. The two appeared together in a group photo from the event.

At the time, neither had publicly suggested that they were romantically involved.

Dating speculation began the following month after Langley and Wetmore were photographed together at the Soggy Dollar Bar in the British Virgin Islands.

Langley and Wetmore reunited onstage on March 10 at the Heart Strings for Hope charity event.

During the event, Langley joined Wetmore for an acoustic performance of his song “Sunburn.” The two sat across from each other with their guitars as they performed the track together.

On September 22, Langley and Wetmore both attended the ninth annual Nashville Songwriter Awards at Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium.

It was a particularly massive night for Langley: “Choosin’ Texas” won Song of the Year at the ceremony.

After the awards, Langley and Wetmore were photographed leaving the Ryman together through a side door.

The following day, multiple sources confirmed to People that the two are dating. Neither Langley nor Wetmore has spoken about the relationship themselves.

Industry observers note that langley and Wetmore appeared to take another trip to the Virgin Islands together. A man dining at a restaurant they went to posted a video of them arriving.

On November 18, Wetmore was asked about his rumored relationship with Langley while attending the 2026 CMA Awards in Nashville.

When People asked who he was cheering for that evening, Wetmore avoided mentioning Langley, instead naming two male country artists.

“Zach Top or Stephen Wilson Jr.,” he joked.

“I freaking love that guy. Both of them,” he added with a laugh.

Langley entered the ceremony with nine nominations, the most of any artist that year. She went home with six awards.

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Sources indicate that uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Recent findings suggest that combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

The Hottest Thing in Nordic Design Right Now? The Vikings

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships.
  • Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.
  • “Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” claims Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norway is a country built on craftsmanship.

Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships. (Not to mention wool, linen, and leather for their unheralded colorful attire.).

Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.

Traditional wool weaving at Viking Valley.

“Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” claims Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley. Even though this Gudvangen-located recreation village debuted a decade ago, Hylland witnessed a recent surge in visitors following this past summer’s FIFA World Cup, where Norway’s Erling Haaland popularized the Viking row as one of the catchiest celebrations of the football tournament.

“We've seen significant growth in interest in Norway,” adds Nelson Oliveira, managing director, Nordics for luxury travel operator Abercrombie & Kent. Launched in 2024, their small group trip itineraries include a visit to the Viking Valley where guests interact with the Viking chieftain, dine in the reindeer-clad, candle-lit dining hall and visit the resident blacksmith, who continues to supply ironworks for the community, including door hinges and locks. “The Viking era is such an important part of Norway’s history, and we wanted to give guests an opportunity to experience that heritage beyond simply visiting a museum,” says Oliveira.

Magnus the blacksmith at Viking Valley.

Outside the village, quotidian Viking-inspired design is flourishing—and notably predates Haaland’s viral row chant. Matilde Brandt, marketing manager of Klesarven, a Viking heritage clothing retailer founded in 2015 by Lene Lorentzen, credits the global interest in historybounding—where elements of historical fashion are incorporated into everyday styles—for the spike in popularity of their Viking-inspired styles.

According to recent reports, “There is so much more to the [Viking] story than bearded men fighting and wearing dark colors,” claims Brandt. Inspired by Hollywood’s enduringly maligned, inaccurate depictions of Viking Age Scandinavia, Klesarven focuses on historically accurate representations of the people living during that age. “Most of them were farmers, fishermen and craftspeople [who] wore bright, colorful clothing and were well put together,” says Brandt.

A Klesarven Frøya linen dress and Favn shawl.

In a recent development, these motifs are realized across Klesarven’s collection of wool sweaters, linen shirts, and riding skirts. One of Klesarven’s most popular designs is the Viking Age apron dress, inspired by a garment reserved for special occasions and ornamented with colorful beads, brooches, and jewelry crafted from silver, gold, and bronze. Women were also buried in these garments. “It keeps history alive,” says Brandt. “In this way, we help preserve old techniques and craftsmanship.”.

Preserving heritage is also a motivation of Runestone’s founders, Sonya and Kim Andre. Having both grown up on a stretch of coastline dotted with Viking history—Sonya from Uddevalla on Sweden’s west coast and her husband, Kim, from Halden, just across the Norwegian border—Runestone was born from a personal “obsession” with Viking culture.

Sources indicate that when the couple began building an online outfitter dedicated to Viking apparel, Norse jewelry, and rune wall art (the alphabet of Viking culture), Sonya recognized the bigger drive: “A lot of the brands out there lean into that ‘dressed up as a Viking’ look,” indicates Sonya. Runestone promises the opposite; born as a way to embrace history through a modern lens with designs, symbols, and styles as “something anyone can wear and connect with, not just a costume,” says Sonya.

“Every design has a real story behind it—a god, a creature, a rune, and we care a lot about getting that story right,” Sonya continues. “We’re carrying forward the spirit of the Vikings more than the actual lifestyle, religion, or the more brutal parts of the history.”.

Every week, Sonya receives emails, primarily from younger folks who are responding to the uptick in social media attention surrounding Viking culture. “They’re asking really specific questions,” she states, like inquiring about the gods—especially Odin, who is widely regarded as the god of wisdom and warfare—and requesting that Sonya point them toward reliable sources instead of pop culture tales.

For the curious travelers who make it to Norway, they have more opportunity than ever to engage with Viking heritage, from active opportunities like Viking Valley and shopping at Klesarven to passive participation at hotels.

Industry observers note that in the northwestern Ålesund region, Storfjord Hotel was built in traditional Norwegian laft style with timber logs and turf roofs (the latter prioritized in Viking times for insulation). On Manshausen Island, located off the coast of northern Norway, the restaurant walls at the eponymous resort are covered with overlapping wooden scales built in the traditional Viking construction. Its groundskeeper team consists of two dozen sheep—an ancient Nordic breed that was kept during the Viking era.

“A hotel can become much more than a beautiful place to stay,” says Linda Gram Egede-Nissen, co-owner and CEO of interior design firm Gathe + Gram. “It can offer guests a subtle introduction to the culture and history of its surroundings.” In Trondheim, the northern city which served as the Viking capital of Norway many centuries ago, Gathe + Gram just completed the design blueprint for Eras, a boutique hotel where every room has its own distinctive name and story rooted in Viking history, mythology, or craftsmanship.

For this project, Gram Egede-Nissen was “particularly fascinated” by the “remarkable precision, complexity and beauty in the detailing” of historic jewelry from the Viking era. Her team translated the shapes, patterns, and proportions of spenne (buckles), skålspenne (ornamental brooches), and polyedrisk (beads) into architectural details and smaller design elements—decorative cushions, sculptural chandeliers, and wall art—throughout the interiors. “There is an incredible richness in the [Viking-era] jewelry—and many of these forms feel surprisingly relevant even today,” says Gram Egede-Nissen.

“To me, that is where heritage becomes truly relevant,” adds Gram Egede-Nissen. “Not when we preserve it as something untouchable, but when we allow it to inspire fresh ideas.”.

How to Grow a Beard

📅 20 Oct 2014 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that so you want to learn how to grow a beard.
  • “I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, indicates.
  • Industry observers note that there’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that so you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.

“I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, indicates. “Your beard needs time to actually show you what it’s going to look like, and that growth period lets you see the natural direction everything’s growing in. Plus, some hairs take longer to come in than others, so patience is key.”.

Industry observers note that there’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack. These are the best tips to maximize your hair follicles’ potential whether this is your first beard or your fiftieth.

Industry observers note that there are many different beard styles to choose from; you don’t need to stick to neatly manicured, uniform look. Let your growth be influenced by the style you want to achieve.

According to recent reports, “Your genes determine hair thickness, growth rate, density, and color,” Mendoza states. “If your dad or granddad had a thin beard, you’re probably dealing with the same hand, and that’s just life.”.

Industry observers note that if your beard is patchy, or if it has a unique growth pattern (sparse on the cheeks, full on the goatee, for example), then you should set your expectations properly. This goes for beards big, small, and medium alike. And while nutrition is important for hair growth, you can’t cheat genetics with your diet.

Recent findings suggest that patience is a virtue. Not only can a little time help fill in some patchiness, but it’s also requisite for almost any style. A beard transforms into something latest every week. So, if it’s seeming like you’ll never reach your goal—in particular if it’s a long beard—then you honestly might wake up one morning and realize that you’ve arrived at the destination.

It has been revealed that mendoza says to wait at least two weeks before you start to do a cleanup, but only around the ends, i.e. the hairs that aren’t within the perimeter in which you want your beard to grow. That’ll help you figure out your beard’s natural shape.

Sources indicate that one of the tenets of beard maintenance is to keep it defined. In short: shave the neckline and clean up the cheek lines. These keep it more beard-like and less neckbeard-like—unless, for some reason, a wooly stoner beard is your aim. In that case, let it grow wild and free.

Industry observers note that the second way to keep things looking intentional is to sculpt and trim your beard as it grows. It might feel counterproductive—and counter to #2—but it’s the same way you need to get haircuts while growing out your hair. As Mendoza notes, this helps direct the hair exactly where it needs to be: Fuller in some spots, less so in others. The styling products in the next tip can of course help influence things, but you foremost want to keep hairs in check as needed: This can mean spot-checking strays, snipping away split ends, or simply taking out some bulk. You’ll want a beard trimmer or a sharp pair of scissors.

Industry observers note that there are a handful of beard products you should consider picking up if you’re serious about proper care and maintenance. A few drops of beard oil will absorb quickly and give your hair the right nutrients (plus a pinch of shine), while also making it less wild and frizzy. You can also swap in a beard balm or cream, something slightly heftier than an oil, to help style the beard and keep it in place all day. What’s notable is that you clean your beard every day with an actual beard wash and not just a regular shampoo, which Mendoza indicates will dry out your beard and your face.

It has been revealed that weekly maintenance will consist of a deep condition, which you can do in the shower. “If you’re doing those things consistently, your beard is going to look way healthier and fuller than most guys out there,” he notes.

Beard brushes help exfoliate the skin beneath the beard, for starters, which lifts dead skin cells and prevents future flaking. Moreover, brushing your beard at the end of each day will ensure its health and tame-ability in the long haul. This distributes the natural oils produced in the skin, which otherwise collect at the base of the shaft and only nourish the bottom of each hair. This oil distribution prevents breakage, frizzing, and split ends. (This is a great time to apply a few drops of beard oil as a booster, especially after a shower.).

In a recent development, once your base has grown out—this can take months—it’s time to really make it yours. One of our favorites is to snip the bridge between the mustache and the chin, thus marooning the mustache. Or, pare back the beard itself, leaving a fuller mustache. You have lots of options, and it’s your privilege as a beard grower to flaunt it.

  • The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Sources indicate that melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

According to recent reports, ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.
